nameStory: The Striped Greenhouse Slug earned its name from the distinctive light and dark bands that run along its body, combined with its notorious reputation as a greenhouse pest. This little mollusk has hitchhiked around the world in plant shipments, making itself at home in the warm, humid conditions of commercial greenhouses. The 'valentianus' part of its scientific name honors the region of Valencia, Spain, though this slug has long since become a true world traveler.
description: The Striped Greenhouse Slug is a small, soft-bodied mollusk that carries no shell on its back like its snail cousins. True to its name, it displays alternating light and dark stripes running lengthwise down its grayish-brown body. These slugs typically reach about 1-2 inches long when fully extended. As members of the keelback slug family, they have a subtle ridge or 'keel' running down their back, giving them a slightly peaked appearance rather than being perfectly rounded.

idTips.label: Striped Pattern
idTips.description: Look for distinctive alternating light and dark stripes running from head to tail along the body - these bands are usually most visible when the slug is moving and stretched out

idTips.label: Keeled Back
idTips.description: Run your finger gently along the back to feel a subtle ridge or keel - it creates a slightly peaked roofline rather than a smooth, rounded dome

idTips.label: Size and Shape
idTips.description: When fully extended, reaches about 1-2 inches long with a relatively slender build compared to chunky garden slugs - feels firm but squishy to the touch

idTips.label: Mucus Trail
idTips.description: Leaves a thin, clear slime trail that feels slightly sticky between your fingers and may have an iridescent sheen in sunlight

idTips.label: Greenhouse Habitat
idTips.description: Most commonly found in greenhouses, garden centers, or around heated buildings where it stays active even in cooler weather

habitat: In New England, Striped Greenhouse Slugs are primarily found in artificial environments like commercial greenhouses, garden centers, and conservatories where temperatures stay warm year-round. They occasionally venture outdoors in summer, hiding under potted plants, in mulched garden beds near buildings, or around compost piles where decomposing organic matter provides both food and shelter. Look for them in moist, protected spots with rich organic soil, especially near human habitation where they can retreat to warmer microclimates.

seasonality.spring: Most active in heated greenhouses and may begin appearing outdoors as temperatures warm, often found under plant pots and in garden centers receiving new plant shipments.
seasonality.summer: Peak outdoor activity when they may venture into gardens and landscaped areas, especially during humid nights and early morning hours when dew keeps surfaces moist.
seasonality.fall: Begin retreating to heated indoor spaces like greenhouses and garden centers, becoming less visible outdoors as temperatures drop below their comfort zone.
seasonality.winter: Primarily active only in heated indoor environments like commercial greenhouses where they continue feeding and breeding regardless of outdoor conditions.

funFact: This slug is basically a stowaway that has accidentally conquered the world - it has spread to every continent except Antarctica simply by hiding in plant shipments, making it one of the most successful accidental travelers in the animal kingdom, rivaling even humans for global distribution!
confusionNotes: Most likely confused with other small garden slugs, but the combination of distinctive striping and greenhouse habitat sets it apart. Memory trick: 'Striped Stowaway' - if you see stripes on a slug in or near a greenhouse or garden center, you've probably found your Striped Greenhouse Slug.
contextualKnowledge: Despite being called a 'greenhouse' slug, this species didn't originally evolve in greenhouses - it's simply adapted so well to these artificial environments that it's become synonymous with them. The scientific name has changed over time (formerly Lehmannia valentiana), which can cause confusion in older field guides and plant pest literature.
compareHints: Since this is the only Ambigolimax species commonly found in New England, compare it with other small keelback slugs in the Limacidae family. Unlike smooth-backed slugs, it has that distinctive keel or ridge, and unlike larger garden slugs, it maintains its slender build and characteristic striping. The greenhouse habitat preference also helps distinguish it from native woodland slug species that avoid human-modified environments.
